extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of analytic geometry and classical mathematical methods (advanced undergraduates / readers of mathematical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Worked exposition solving the problem of a sphere tangent to four given spheres (and related special cases and reciprocal relations), followed by a tutorial on the method of (conditional) multipliers (Lagrange multipliers) and material on conjugate diameters for second-order curves and surfaces. Presents procedures, formulae, and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equations of tangency for a sphere touching four given spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate equations from squared distances between centers and radii so that (R + r_i)^2 equals squared distance between centres; use subtraction of pairs, algebraic reduction, division by common factors (e.g. a^2 or (r_i + r_j)^2), and substitutions to obtain linear/quadratic relations determining the centre coordinates and reciprocal of the radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page shows deriving equations (e.g. (13), (26), (28)) by subtracting and reducing squared-distance relations, dividing by a' or (r_i + r_j)^2, then simplifying by substitutions (notation like s, p in (29),(30)) so that the co-ordinates x,y,z and the reciprocal of the radius are determined. Follow the algebraic elimination steps, restore reciprocals at the end, and solve the final polynomial (e.g. equate products to squares as done before (34)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external tangency substitution rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain the sphere touched internally by given spheres, write the difference of the radii instead of their sum in the tangency equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit instruction: 'the magnitude and position of the sphere touched internally by four spheres in mutual contact, may be deduced at once from the preceding investigation. For in this case we have simply to write in the equations (7, 8, 9, 10) the difference of the radii instead of their sum.' Practically, replace (r + r_i) by (R - r_i) or equivalently use negative r_i in formulas as noted in the footnote to (37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane as limiting sphere (plane as sphere of infinite radius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat a plane as a sphere of indefinitely great radius when one of the tangent objects is a plane, by taking the corresponding radius to infinity in the sphere-formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: in the general formulae (e.g. (35)), let one radius tend to infinity and simplify the notation (see text around equation (68)). The resulting formulae give the radius and centre co-ordinates for a sphere tangent to three given spheres and a plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-radius relation for six mutually tangent spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: If four spheres are in mutual contact and two others are described to be touched by all four internally and externally, then the reciprocal of the radius of the least (inscribed) sphere equals the sum of the reciprocals of the other five.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by subtracting the internal and external reciprocal formulae (equations (38) and (37)) and substituting values; the page states the theorem explicitly and shows its algebraic derivation. Use the sign convention noted: taking plus/minus in certain formulae yields the two reciprocal values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special equal-radii simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When the four given spheres have equal radii, the general formulas reduce to simpler expressions: the inscribed/circumscribed reciprocal radii simplify (see (42),(43)), centres coincide, and remarkable product/sum relations hold (e.g., square of common radius equals twice product of inscribed and circumscribed radii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specialized formulae given for r1=r2=r3=r4 (equations (42)–(45), etc.). The text explains how many cross-terms vanish and gives the simplified relations and coordinates (e.g. (44)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic elimination strategy for radii and centres (alternate derivations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple elimination routes are valid: eliminate z via linear combinations, substitute expressions for x,y into radius equation, or set up an equation whose square equals a product to solve for R; alternative manipulations give the same final reciprocal expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text offers several methods (see derivations around (11)–(18), (29)–(31)) and notes equivalence of results. Follow algebraic elimination, use convenient substitutions (m,n,p notation), and verify consistency among methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional multipliers method (Lagrange multipliers) — core procedural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To find extrema of a function subject to constraint equations: differentiate the function and each constraint; form a combined equation by multiplying constraints by multipliers and adding to the differential of the function; then make coefficients of differentials of the independent variables zero to yield equations for multipliers and variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The section frames the method: multiply constraint(s) by multipliers X, X_i and add to the differential of the target function (see (3),(4)); because the combined equation must hold for the same solutions, require that coefficients of differentials vanish. Examples 1–6 illustrate implementation (linear systems, maximizing volume in ellipsoid, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: use 'conditional multipliers' instead of 'indeterminate multipliers'
rubrics_metrics.description: Multipliers are subject to conditions arising from making the combined differential equation enforce the original constraints; hence they are not truly indeterminate but conditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advocates calling them conditional multipliers because their values are determined by the conditions imposed to eliminate differentials and obtain the necessary number of equations (see discussion preceding examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing multipliers and matching multiplication factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming multiplier equations one must choose quantities by which to multiply the coefficient-equations so that terms align with corresponding terms in the constraint equation; the multipliers and these chosen factors must be consistent with the structure of the constraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote and examples explain that the quantities by which the equations are multiplied must be determined by the proposed equations of condition (see footnote after example 4). For instance, multiply derivative conditions by x,y,z when the constraint has terms x^2,y^2,z^2 to create matching products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application examples as procedural templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete worked examples illustrate the method: (1) solving two/three linear equations via multipliers; (2) maximizing volume of rectangular parallelepiped in an ellipsoid by taking logarithm, differentiating, applying multipliers, equating coefficients to zero, and using constraint to solve; (3) other optimization examples with logarithms and powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the same sequence in each example: take log if helpful, differentiate objective and constraint(s), form combined equation with multipliers, set differential-coefficients to zero, solve for multipliers, then for variables. The page gives numeric specifics (see example computations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and construction of conjugate polars and conjugate diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjugate system pairs points and lines (or points and planes in space) so that to each point of one system there is a corresponding line/plane of the other and vice versa; the polar of a point relative to a conic is given by formula (6) and coefficients are linear functions of the point coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find the pole of a given polar line, equate the coefficients of like powers in the polar equation and the general polar (see (2) and (6)). The poles of all lines parallel to a given line lie on a straight line (the conjugate diameter). Analogous constructions apply in space (planes and poles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for two lines to be conjugate w.r.t. a conic
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two lines y = p x + g and y = p' x + g', they are conjugate with respect to the conic ay^2 + bxy + cx^2 + dy + ex + f = 0 if 2 a p p' + b(p + p') + 2 c = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by equating coefficients in polar relation (see worked derivation around (7)). Use this algebraic condition to test conjugacy of directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common intersection point of conjugate diameters for family of conics
rubrics_metrics.description: For an infinite family of conics of the second degree passing through four given points, the diameters conjugate to sections parallel to a fixed line all intersect at the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via writing the conjugate condition (equation like (9)) which contains an arbitrary coefficient; solving the resulting linear system in x,y yields a single intersection point common to all diameters. The page extends the idea to space (surfaces through eight points).
